title: Deterministic Simulation Testing
summary: Explore many hostile executions, but make every failure exactly replayable — building deterministic simulation testing from the determinism contract up to a shrunk, permanently-regressed bug.

concepts.title: Why Conventional Testing Fails
concepts.brief: Heisenbugs, race conditions, timing dependencies, partial failure, flaky tests. Why chaos engineering, fuzzing, integration tests, model checking, and DST overlap but are not substitutes. The value proposition: a failing seed becomes a durable regression test.

concepts.title: The Determinism Contract
concepts.brief: Sources of nondeterminism: wall clocks, timers, random numbers, scheduling, network delivery, disk persistence, process identity, external APIs. Seeded pseudo-randomness versus uncontrolled randomness. Deterministic replay, trace capture, event logs, snapshots, and replay compatibility across code changes. Logical time, virtual time, and discrete-event scheduling.

concepts.title: Architectures for DST
concepts.brief: Simulation-first / in-process: abstract I/O behind interfaces and run real application logic against simulated network, storage, time, and randomness. Virtualization-first: run ordinary containers or processes under a deterministic hypervisor. Trade-offs: fidelity, implementation cost, throughput, dependency control, language/runtime constraints. Designing systems for simulation: dependency injection, ports/adapters, explicit clocks and RNGs, avoiding hidden global state.

concepts.title: Building the Simulator
concepts.brief: Event queues, actors/state machines, cooperative concurrency, deterministic schedulers. Simulated network: delay, loss, duplication, reordering, partitions, asymmetric reachability. Simulated disks: durability boundaries, partial writes, corruption, full disks, latency. Process/node lifecycle: crash, pause, reboot, slow node, configuration change. Time semantics: timers, deadlines, leases, clock skew and jumps.

concepts.title: Workloads & State-Space Exploration
concepts.brief: Generative/property-based workloads versus hand-authored scenarios. Input generation, seed management, shrinking/minimizing a failing execution. Scheduling and fault distributions, combinatorial explosion, coverage and novelty heuristics. Swarm testing: vary cluster topology, replication, feature flags, workloads, and fault profiles per run. Buggification: deliberately selecting rare but valid outcomes — spurious errors, unusual timing, boundary configuration values.

concepts.title: Oracles: Deciding Whether a Run Is Correct
concepts.brief: Local assertions and runtime invariants. End-to-end safety properties: no lost committed writes, no double-spend, uniqueness, ordering, linearizability/serializability. Liveness and recovery: once the environment becomes healthy, the system eventually converges or serves requests. Reference models, shadow implementations, metamorphic tests, history checking. The vital distinction between an observed symptom and a correctness oracle.

concepts.title: Fault Models
concepts.brief: Crash-stop versus crash-recovery assumptions. Network partitions, packet faults, latency, bandwidth/CPU throttling. Storage semantics, durability lies, disk-full behavior, metadata corruption. Clock failures, DNS/configuration failures, dependency failures. Fault realism: how to avoid absurd fault combinations while preserving adversarial power. Antithesis's fault taxonomy (network, node, clock, thread pausing, CPU modulation) makes an excellent table here.

concepts.title: Debugging & Developer Workflow
concepts.brief: Failure artifacts: seed, configuration, event trace, logs, assertion history, fault timeline. Time travel, checkpoints, binary search through execution, causal slicing. Turning minimized failures into fast CI regressions. Determinism-preserving observability — adding logs without changing the schedule. CI strategy: per-PR smoke DST, nightly seed farms, pre-release bursts, failure triage.

concepts.title: Limits & Complementary Techniques
concepts.brief: What DST does not validate well: real hardware behavior, production performance, OS/filesystem contract misunderstandings, third-party black boxes. Combining DST with real-cluster performance tests, hardware fault testing, production observability, and formal methods. Simulator fidelity and the 'simulation gap'. Cost/ROI and an incremental adoption roadmap for an existing service.

concepts.title: Hands-On Capstone
concepts.brief: Implement a small replicated key-value store, job queue, or payment ledger simulator. Add deterministic time, a seeded scheduler, network partitions, crash/restart, and a state-machine reference oracle. Find, shrink, replay, fix, and permanently regress a deliberately planted bug. Especially compelling with a Rust implementation — traits for Clock, Network, Storage and Random; or an Elixir version based on deterministic message delivery and process supervision.

images.prompt: A hand-drawn practice-notebook sketch: ballpoint linework with red-pen annotation on cream ruled paper, slightly imperfect strokes, hand-lettered arrows and margin marks, a hint of tape or paper-clip realism. Warm and informal — obviously drawn by a person, not rendered. Subject: on the left margin, one small circled dot labeled "seed" in red pen; from it, several thin ballpoint lines fan rightward and branch repeatedly like a tree of diverging timelines, each branch passing through small hand-drawn glyphs suggesting trouble (a jagged lightning bolt for a crash, a broken line for a network partition, a tiny clock with a bent hand for clock skew); one branch near the bottom is circled in red pen with a small red arrow looping back to the original seed dot, annotated "replay ↺" — the idea that a hostile run can be traced back to its exact cause. Generous whitespace, no other text baked in beyond the two short labels described. Target size ~1280×720px, 16:9 landscape; compose for a small on-page figure with the subject centred and safe margins — it is letterboxed into a 16:9 box, so keep nothing important near the edges.
